system_instruction: You are applying A Philosophy of Software Design principles to software architecture decisions. Use these 15 principles to evaluate designs, identify complexity, and recommend refactoring strategies.

quick_reference.core_insight: Complexity is the enemy. Strategic design investments (10-20% time) pay for themselves in 6-18 months through faster development.

principles.statement: Complexity is anything that makes software hard to understand and modify. It increases development time exponentially.
principles.reasoning: Developers spend time understanding code. Complex code requires understanding more. Complexity multiplies across team.
principles.when_to_use: Every design decision. Measure: Do small changes require modifications in many places? If yes: complexity problem.
principles.bad_example: Website with banner color hardcoded on 100 pages. Change color = 100 changes.
principles.good_example: Color defined in one place. Change color = 1 change.

principles.principle: Dependencies and Obscurity are Complexity's Causes
principles.statement: Complexity caused by: dependencies (change amplification) and obscurity (unknown unknowns).
principles.reasoning: Dependencies require coordinated changes. Obscurity hides what needs changing.

principles.statement: Tactical: hack out features fast, defer design. Strategic: invest 10-20% in design upfront.
principles.reasoning: Tactical creates compounding technical debt. Strategic pays for itself in 6-18 months.
principles.when_to_use: Every sprint. Allocate 10-20% time for design/refactoring.

principles.statement: Module depth = (functionality provided) / (interface complexity). Deep modules provide maximum value.
principles.reasoning: Deep modules reusable; shallow modules copied or wrapped, adding complexity.
principles.bad_example: Java I/O: FileInputStream + BufferedInputStream + ObjectInputStream = 3 objects for reading file
principles.good_example: Unix I/O: 5 functions (open, read, write, seek, close) hiding 100k+ lines

principles.statement: Each module encapsulates design decisions. Knowledge embedded in implementation, not exposed in interface.
principles.reasoning: Simplifies interfaces; makes systems easier to evolve.

principles.principle: Information Leakage is a Red Flag
principles.statement: Information leakage: same knowledge used in multiple places. Back-door leakage (hidden) worse than interface leakage.
principles.reasoning: Creates dependencies between modules. Change one = break others.

principles.statement: Organize code by knowledge, not by execution order.
General-purpose interfaces tend to be deeper than special-purpose interfaces.
principles.reasoning: Generality enables reuse; specialization requires workarounds.

principles.statement: Best way to eliminate exception handling complexity: redefine APIs so errors don't exist.
principles.reasoning: Exception handling code is complex and buggy.

principles.statement: Obvious code: readers understand it quickly without deep analysis.
principles.reasoning: Nonobvious code increases bugs and development time.

principles.statement: Precise names clarify behavior. Consistent patterns enable recognition.
principles.reasoning: Good names reduce cognitive load. Consistency eliminates learning curves.
principles.when_to_use: For every variable, method, class name.

principles.principle: Comments Are Essential for Deeper Modules
principles.statement: Comments explain what code cannot: why, intent, non-obvious behavior.
principles.reasoning: Good comments save 10x time in understanding.
principles.when_to_use: For classes, complex methods, design decisions.

principles.statement: Consider multiple alternatives before implementing. Second design reveals trade-offs.
principles.reasoning: Multiple designs force consideration of trade-offs.
principles.when_to_use: Before implementing big features or new modules.

principles.statement: If something complicated, module should do work, not callers.
principles.reasoning: Pushing complexity to callers multiplies it.
key_rules: Don't make callers handle edge cases

principles.principle: Invest 10-20% Time in Design, Not Features
principles.reasoning: Investment pays for itself in 6-18 months through faster development.

faq.question: How do I know if my code is too complex?
faq.answer: Red flags: (1) Small changes require modifications in many places, (2) Developers must understand large portions to make changes, (3) Hidden knowledge you don't know exists

faq.question: Is it worth spending 10-20% time on design?
faq.answer: Yes. Investment pays for itself in 6-18 months through faster future development. Long-term productivity >> short-term velocity.

faq.question: When should I refactor?
faq.answer: When complexity is slowing down development. Priority: by frequency of changes to that module.
